author: Amira El-Fekki
title: ‘Staying on Warraq’: Residents formally demand land within New Warraq City redevelopment plan
content:
Dozens of Warraq Island residents submitted a formal list of demands to authorities on Tuesday concerning their right to remain and be allocated their own land within the state’s development project on the island, several residents who participated told Mada Masr.


The move marked a collective step to demand the government guarantee their right to remain and ensure they have the resources to do so —  the latest in a series of efforts residents have undertaken to confront authorities over the nine years since the government sought to evacuate them by force to attract foreign investment to develop the Nile island. Security restrictions have squeezed their resources over the intervening years and led to a deterioration in living conditions. 


Top of those demands was a request for land within the redevelopment area to be specifically designated for residents who have chosen to stay to build their own homes. The residents called for a clear timeline for the implementation of the rehousing scheme, with defined mechanisms and fair conditions.


They also demanded the dismissal of all lawsuits filed against the younger residents tied to security incidents that have taken place in response to attempts to remove people from the island. 


Residents delivered their written demands in person to a representative of the New Warraq City Development headquarters, where a heavy security deployment was present, across the island and at its entrances, one of the residents in attendance said to Mada Masr on condition of anonymity.


The source said the handover took place without incident, “because we came to demand legitimate rights.”


Mada Masr has reached out to the Housing Ministry’s spokesperson for comment but did not receive a response at the time of writing.


The residents also called for urgent improvements to daily life, pending progress on their main demands, including a primary healthcare unit that provides essential medicines and medical services, the restoration of the youth sports center and postal services, the removal of construction waste and the restoration of affordable sewage pumping services.


They further demanded the organized entry of construction materials and the removal of the security checkpoints at the island’s ferry crossings, saying the measures would help prevent recurring clashes between residents and police.


Clashes between security forces and dozens of residents broke out again on the island

this month

 near the Qolaly ferry crossing, where a security officer assaulted a boy bringing building materials onto the island. The clashes lasted several days, with three protesters arrested and later released. 


Amid ongoing

tensions

 over the state’s New Warraq City project and efforts to expropriate land and evict residents, restrictions on bringing construction materials onto the island have intensified in recent months, with materials allowed only in limited quantities and with security approval or otherwise smuggled in.


As confrontations escalated in August, residents held a

one-day sit-in

 at the crossing the

government

was using to transport construction material, which ended after security authorities promised to organize the entry of construction materials for the residents. The Housing Ministry

denied

 days later that the New Warraq Island Development Authority had permitted the delivery of any construction materials or supplies to enter the island.


Frustrated with the restrictions, Warraq residents launched the “Staying on the land” campaign on Friday, the latest in a series of attempts by residents to organize against the state’s development project and its accompanying expropriations and home evictions, dating back to the formation of the island’s family council in 2017. 


“What we receive are merely informal promises that our demands are being considered, and nearly 10 years have passed,” the statement read. “During that time, we have seen state agencies take measures aimed at putting pressure on island residents to force us to leave our homes,” residents said in a Friday statement following their first meeting.


They said they have addressed several government bodies, including agencies affiliated with the Armed Forces Engineering Authority and the police, but that they had received no official response. 


On Tuesday, residents gave authorities one week to provide an official response, with one of their main demands being direct communication with a government official …

author: Paul Tiyambe Zeleza
title: Who Killed Jason Arday?
content:
Earlier this afternoon, my oldest boyhood friend, a distinguished international lawyer who received his doctorate at Cambridge, called me to share the tragic news that Jason Arday, the Black British academic, had been found dead. I have been following this story ever since it broke out in July. We commiserated about his tragic death, and concluded that Arday was killed by many people and institutions.


Jason Arday’s death was the result of a convergence of forces that reveal the fragility of the racial settlement in post-imperial and postcolonial Britain and the contradictions of its elite institutions. He was eagerly elevated as a symbol, ruthlessly scrutinized as an anomaly, and callously discarded as a liability. His rise and fall expose the moral bankruptcy of a system that wants the appearance of racial progress without the work of structural change.


Arday was killed by white liberal proponents of performative inclusion who propelled him, shrouding him with the aura of heroic exceptionalism. Cambridge presented him as its youngest Black professor and celebrated his life story as proof of institutional transformation. His appointment was marketed through a narrative of adversity and triumph that emphasized his autism, late speech, poverty, and extraordinary athletic feats. This pattern reflects what Musa al‑Gharbi identifies in his provocative book, We Have Never Been Woke: The Cultural Contradictions of a New Elite as the behavior of white liberal symbolic capitalists, a highly educated professional class that converts the visibility of marginalized individuals into moral and cultural currency. In al‑Gharbi’s analysis, elite “wokeness” functions as a prestige economy in which institutions and their leaders signal virtue through symbolic gestures that flatter their self‑image while leaving material inequalities untouched. Cambridge embraced Arday as a form of symbolic capital, a figure whose improbable ascent could be displayed as evidence of moral renewal without requiring structural reform.


Tyler Austin Harper’s critique of elite academic hypocrisy in a recent issue of The Atlantic further illuminates this dynamic. Harper argues that universities deploy progressive rhetoric as a cheap moral shield to obscure exploitative labor practices, administrative bloat, and declining faculty security. In his account, institutions perform inclusion through branding and narrative while practicing exclusion through precarity, union‑busting, and corporate governance. Cambridge’s elevation of Arday fits this model of “inclusive exclusion,” where symbolic diversity is celebrated even as the underlying structures remain unchanged. This environment encouraged a celebratory gaze that focused on Arday’s biography rather than his scholarship, allowing mythmaking to substitute for rigorous evaluation and creating conditions in which his elevation served institutional needs more than his own.


The university killed Arday. Cambridge used his biography as a public relations asset. The institution did not conduct basic due diligence on his academic record, his claims, or his CV. Senior academics later admitted they had never heard of his work. Cambridge’s vice chancellor now acknowledges that the appointment process was flawed and that the faculty of education bears responsibility for the errors in a classic maneuver of institutional leadership deflection and passing the buck. Nearly one hundred senior academics demanded an independent investigation, noting that the appointment had been made not by the faculty but by a separate board of electors chaired by university leadership.


The institutional response intensified the damage. Cambridge initially defended him as the victim of a smear campaign. When pressure mounted, the university reversed course and announced a new investigation. It deleted webpages and removed references to his work. Jesus College ended its inquiry the moment his resignation terminated his fellowship. Cambridge’s leadership now concedes that the case has damaged the institution. The university’s actions reveal a pattern of reputational self-protection that abandons individuals once they cease to serve institutional interests.


The media killed Arday. The scrutiny that followed his appointment was immediate and intense. Allegations of plagiarism surfaced through Nathan Cofnas, a self-described “race realist” who has argued that Black people would disappear from high-profile positions at top universities …

author: Ezzat Khairi
title: Sudan: Burhan’s Dialogue Is Not a Path to Stability
content:
General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has discovered dialogue again. After years of promises, a military coup, emergency rule, war rhetoric and political exclusion, Sudan’s army chief now says he wants a comprehensive dialogue inside the country to complete a civilian democratic transition.

Al Jazeera

 reported proposals to drop death-penalty charges against opposition leaders and form a preparatory committee;

Radio Dabanga

 reported talk of a presidential amnesty for leaders of the Civil Democratic Alliance, known as Somoud, and other political activists.


The language is familiar. That is precisely the problem.


Since 2019, Burhan has repeatedly presented himself as Sudan’s temporary guardian on the road to civilian rule. After the previous military President Omar al-Bashir was overthrown in 2019, Burhan promised a civilian government and a transition of no more than two years, as

Reuters

 reported at the time. In October 2021, however, Burhan led a new military takeover that dissolved the civilian-led government, imposed emergency rule and saw Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok detained;

Human Rights Watch

 documented the rights implications of that takeover. In 2022, Burhan again said the army would step back from politics, a pledge reported by

Al Jazeera

. By 2023 and 2024, once war had erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces led by General Burhan and the Rapid Support Forces led by Muhammad Hamdan Dagalo (‘Hemedti’), Burhan was ruling out negotiations and promising decisive victory, according to

Reuters

 and

Sudan Tribune

.


Now, after failing to win the war, failing to restore the state, and failing to build a stable political order even in territories under army control, Burhan returns to the word ‘dialogue’ as if words have no memory.


Sudan’s crisis is not a shortage of conferences. It is a surplus of armed men trying to use civilians as witnesses to arrangements already written by force. Burhan’s latest invitation should therefore be read less as a democratic opening than as a political maneuver. It seeks to transform battlefield survival into political legitimacy by drawing civilian democratic forces into a process designed under military authority, inside army-controlled territory, while coercive institutions remain in the hands of the same power that derailed the transition.


This is not dialogue. It is managed consent.


General Burhan and US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo in 2020 when Burhan chaired the Transitional Sovereignty Council during a period of power sharing between the military and a civilian Cabinet of Ministers (2019-21).


The contradiction is stark. Burhan speaks of democratic transition while insisting that dialogue be held inside Sudan under a wartime authority that decides who is ‘national’ and who is excluded. He speaks of civilian rule while preserving the military’s right to define politics. He speaks of sovereignty while presiding over a war drawn into foreign interests and regional rivalries.


The question is not whether Sudanese should talk. Of course they should. The question is who sets the table, who holds the gun outside the door, and whether civilians are invited to shape a transition or merely to decorate one.


This is why Burhan’s offer is structurally weak. As I argued in

African Arguments

, Sudan’s war is no longer a simple two-sided contest between a national army and a paramilitary rebellion. Burhan and Hemedti, lead coalitions, not unified institutions. The SAF camp includes regular units, Darfuri armed movements, local defence groups and Islamist-linked networks that see the army’s survival as a route back to power. Any real settlement would require one national army, civilian oversight, exclusion of former-regime networks and accountability. Each step threatens a constituency on which Burhan depends.


The weakness is visible in areas under army control. Military recovery has not become political restoration.

Reuters

 reported in July 2026 that more than two million people had returned to Khartoum while electricity operated at about one-third of prewar capacity. Nor has army control delivered security.

Reuters

 reported drone strikes on Khartoum airport and other targets

in May 2026

, renewed RSF pressure on al-Obeid and drone strikes in the wider capital

in August 2026

; and attacks on Port Sudan

in 2025

 that targeted fuel depots and which put aid deliveries at risk. A government that cannot secure its wartime capital, restore basic …

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Marikana’s wounds still bleed 14 years after police massacre
content:
Fourteen years after police opened fire on striking mineworkers at Marikana, the massacre is remembered not only for the 34 men who were killed, but for their absence in the lives of their families.


For some, the memory is of a father who never came home. For others, it is the loss of a breadwinner, a brother or a son. And for those who were children when the killings happened, it is the experience of growing up with memories that have become increasingly distant, while the questions about justice remain.


At a commemoration marking 14 years since the massacre, the families, activists and academics reflected on what Marikana means more than a decade later – and on its place in South Africa’s longer history of protest, police violence and struggles for dignity.


For the Socio-Economic Rights Institute of South Africa (Seri), which has represented the families since 2012, the central question remains accountability. Seri secured payments for 35 of the 37 families whose loved ones were killed by police. Two families have received no compensation.


Seri’s executive director, Nomzamo Zondo said the compensation process itself reflected a deeper problem in how the state understood the loss suffered by the families. “Part of that is a narrative that what the state is interested in compensating is the income that the miners would have earned. They do not want to account for the husbands, brothers, sons and fathers that they took away from the families,” she said.


For Zondo, compensation alone cannot address the significance of Marikana. The state also needs to acknowledge that the massacre should never have happened, she argued: “That’s what a public holiday on the 16

th

 of August would mean. It would say: we are saying never, never again.”


She said this was particularly important given the continued use of force by police in managing protests. “We’ve seen that police continue to manage protests through the use of violence. They have continuously refused to accept that their role is to facilitate protests as a constitutional right.”


Zondo also pointed to the failure to implement recommendations made by the panel of experts on public order policing and the management of protests. The panel completed its work in 2018, but its recommendations remain largely unimplemented.


Squalid living conditions in the informal settlement, Nkaneng, in the shadow of Marikana platinum mine, a source of immense wealth for the owners in 2012, Lonmin. Archive photo by The Benchmarks Foundation


Another major concern, she said, was the failure of the National Prosecuting Authority to bring those responsible for the 16 August killings to court. “Every year, of course, when the anniversary comes, there is an explanation that work is being done,” Zondo said. “But now we are like one year short from 15 years since the massacre. We are just 12 years since the Commission finalised its report and recommended that the NPA must investigate and charge whoever is responsible.”


The question, she said, was whether there was “really an intention to hold anyone accountable for the deaths of the 16

th

 of August”.


For the families, however, the consequences of Marikana are not measured only by the progress of criminal investigations or compensation claims. They are lived in the absence of loved ones.


‘I still have that memory’


NowilI Nungu was 15 when her father, Jackson Lehopa, was killed at Marikana. Today, at 29, she remembers him through the ordinary moments of their life together: travelling to school on a bicycle, buying him a Coke and watching him repair the bicycle whenever it broke.


“I have so many memories with my dad,” Nungu said. She was the only girl among six children and had been living with her father in Rustenburg while her mother moved back to the Eastern Cape.


By the time of the massacre, Nungu had moved to the Eastern Cape with her mother. The family did not have electricity and relied on the radio for news. Her father normally called every day after returning from the koppie to tell them he was safe. But that day, he did not call.


Crosses erected at the koppie as a symbol of lives lost on 16 August 2012. Archive photo by Muzi Mzoyi


Sebolai Liau lost his father, the late Janefeke Raphael Liau, at Marikana. For him, the question of justice remains unresolved. “I think regarding the Marikana massacre, there is no justice. I don’t think it will ever be served, but for now it has not been, and there are no signs …

author: Abahlali_3
title: This August we honour the women of South Africa
content:
11 August 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Press Statement

This August we honour the women of South Africa

This August, in women’s month, we speak of the comrades who are mothers, daughters, sisters and grandmothers, comrades who wake up every morning in the shack settlements and carry the weight of a country that has forgotten them.

We honour the women who keep their families going under conditions of brutal impoverishment and the women who resist oppression. We honour the women in our movement.

But this is not a month of celebration.

No woman is fully free in South Africa. All women are at risk of violence. Impoverished women remain profoundly oppressed.

There is no celebration when women continue to live under very dangerous conditions.

There is no celebration when a woman must walk to a communal tap after dark and risk rape or attack.

There is no celebration when there is no electricity, no running water, no toilets, and no safety for children.

There is no celebration when a woman does not know if her home will be standing tomorrow because of evictions, fires, or political violence.

For millions of impoverished women in shacks, tin houses and backyards, every day is a fight for survival.

To celebrate while all this is true is to lie.

This August we honour all the women of our movement who refused to accept poverty as fate.

We honour Nqobile Nzuza who was murdered by a police officer on a road blockade in Cato Crest on 30 September 2013. She was seventeen years old and doing her matric. She joined the road blockade in protest against the brutal attacks on the Marikana Land Occupation in Cato Manor by the eThekwini Municipality. She was committed to the struggle for land.

We honour Comrade Thuli Ndlovu, a leader of Abahlali baseMjondolo in KwaNdengezi. She fought for land, for housing, and for the dignity of her community. She was assassinated on 27 September 2014 for confronting oppression.

We honour Comrade Nokuthula Mabaso, a leader of eKhenana Commune and of the Abahlali Women’s League. She was a mother, an organiser, and a builder of a community that fed itself and governed itself. She was assassinated on 5 May 2022 while her community was under attack. She knew that poor people must seize the right to land and to live with dignity.

Our brave comrades refused oppression and insisted on land and dignity. Thuli and Nokuthula were leaders.

We also honour other women who have given their lives in the struggle for justice.

Fikile Ntshangase was a leading member of the Mfolozi Community Environmental Justice Organisation (MCEJO) which opposed the destruction of people’s land and homes by coal mining. She was assassinated on 22 October 2020.

Babita Deokaran was an honest civil servant and a whistleblower in the Gauteng Department of Health. She exposed corruption and the theft of public money meant for the public hospitals and clinics that serve the poor. She was assassinated in 2021 for refusing to look away as powerful and dangerous men looted the healthcare system.

We have no interest in politicians who come with speeches and flowers and say nothing about the oppression we live today and nothing about our leaders who have given their lives in the struggle against this oppression.

1.⁠ ⁠Secure access to land and decent housing so no woman sleeps in fear of eviction or fire. 2.⁠ Access to basic services such as water, electricity, sanitation, and safe public lighting in every settlement. 3.⁠ ⁠An end to political killings and intimidation of women organisers. 4.⁠ ⁠An end to gender-based violence in homes, streets, schools and communities. 5.⁠ ⁠Decent work, healthcare and education so women are not forced to choose between feeding their children and their own health. 6. Reproductive healthcare and contraception available without humiliation or delay. 7. A livable guaranteed income in recognition of the unpaid care work that holds families and communities together. 8. Decisive action to reduce food prices on essential items. 9. An end to attempts to turn poor women against migrant and refugee women, since the enemy is landlessness, unemployment and state neglect, not our neighbours. 10.⁠ ⁠Accountability for the killings of Nqobile, Thuli, Nokuthula, Fikile, Babita and all the other murdered and assassinated women activists whose cases were closed and forgotten.

Poor women are not asking to be celebrated. We are demanding to be safe, to be housed, to be heard, to be alive.

Until that happens, August …

author: William Shoki
title: On Safari
content:
Ever since the

World Cup

 concluded with Spain’s emphatic triumph over universally loathed Argentina (at least it felt this way), it has no longer felt like everyone is looking in the same direction at the same time. For a month and a bit, football’s biggest stage gave us one of the last remaining experiences of shared, global time. Not global justice, not global equality — the tournament is in many ways a monument to their absence — but a crude, synchronized schedule. Games at set hours, short-lived solidarities, the impression, however false, that the world is briefly doing something together, undergoing a collective experience.

Once that all ends, you’re plunged back into a social temporality and news cycle that moves at lightning speed and adjusting back is disorienting. It didn’t help that I had to deal with a debilitating case of

cyclosporiasis

 (in an ill-fated decision, I tried some Taco Bell for the first time the day before my return flight back to South Africa, and getting a food-borne illness felt like an appropriate parting gift from a United States in decline). In the weeks since the World Cup, I found myself in a kind of fog I at first attributed to being exhausted from a busy year coupled with bouts of illness, but which, as I return to relatively decent health, I recognize as a familiar feeling, one that has typified contemporary experience for as long as I can remember.

There’s a book by the Polish sociologist Zygmunt Bauman which I think is underrated, and does better at capturing the texture of our epoch than many other attempts (do we live in late capitalism, surveillance capitalism, the burnout society, post-modernity, etc etc.). It’s called

Liquid Modernity

, and Bauman’s straightforward argument is that the defining feature of contemporary society is no longer the construction of stable institutions, identities, and social relationships, but their constant dissolution. Where the “solid” phase of modernity sought to build enduring structures — stable careers, lifelong marriages, nation-states, political parties, class identities, and fixed moral frameworks — our present condition is “liquid”: forms no longer retain their shape for long enough to organize human life. The contradictory result of this is that even though in many important respects, individuals have unprecedented freedom (at least compared to any other point in human history), it’s coupled with chronic insecurity and the burden of constantly having to remake ourselves.

One of his most evocative concepts is the notion of pointillist time, which is “more prominent for its inconsistency and lack of cohesion than for its elements of continuity and consistency.” Time under liquid modernity is fragmented and disconnected, and rather than unfolding as a series of events with some relationship to each other, it is rather a series of “eternal instants.” It’s not hard work to see how this characterizes so much of algorithm-dominated society in general, and our media consumption in particular. If it wasn’t hard enough figuring out what producing any meaningful “content” takes in the attention economy, it was dismaying for me to recently learn that even new media like podcasts and video essays are themselves now being repurposed in a

“clipping economy”

 where increasingly, circulation of short clips from longer pieces is becoming the main event rather than previews.

At

Africa Is a Country

, we are very proud of our World Cup Road Trip series. Three episodes are live —

Episode 1

 on the Cabo Verdean diaspora in New England,

Episode 2

 on the affinity between Algeria and Lawrence, Kansas, and

Episode 3

 on Toronto’s Ghanaian community — with further episodes from the road currently in post-production. Although the website and our weekly newsletters remain our bread and butter, like most outlets, we are experimenting with different ways of reaching audiences, and short-form video has been one of them. The newsletter in particular functions as our most reliable direct channel to readers as social platform referrals grow less dependable. The World Cup, however, gave us a powerful on-ramp: sport brought in readers who might not otherwise arrive at a piece on visa regimes or xenophobia, and the coverage was built to convert that interest into political understanding.

What has been challenging is that discovery is now heavily platform-dependent, and the same work travels very differently depending on where it lands: our road trip …

author: ROAPE
title: The extraversion of African academic journals
content:
There is a long history of donor funding for African universities, research and publishing, going back to the colonial period, and the foundation of the International African Institute in 1926. The crises of higher education and knowledge flows of the 1980s, described by the historian of Africa Michael Crowder as a ‘book famine’, led to a plethora of donor-funded initiatives in support of African journals, book publishing and donations. New publishing NGOs were established including the International Network for the Availability of Scientific Publication and African Journals Online (AJOL). Later, other NGOs promoting access to Northern published journals included the Dutch-based Electronic Information for Libraries (EIFL) and the Research4Life (R4L) partnership funded by UN agencies and several of the major commercial publishers including the largest scientific publisher Elsevier.


Although these NGOs have increased access to online publishing, and to journals published by the commercial presses, they have not strengthened the economic sustainability of African journals. Over 25 years after the launch of these NGOs, African journals remain as dependent on donor funding as they were at inception. Digital discoverability tools, submission platforms, and publishing standards have rapidly evolved, making traditional print publishing obsolete, marginalising journals, and reinforcing knowledge hierarchies.


Dependency and extraversion


Hountondji understood dependency as a condition created by the capitalist core, colonial or metropolitan centres, over the colonial peripheries. This has underpinned the extraversion of scientific publishing and dependency on development donors. As Hountondji foresaw, the science communication system reinforces extraversion and dependency. 


Well before the promises of the internet economy and debates about digital or data colonialism, Hountondji

wrote

 that scientific infrastructure on the continent mainly served to facilitate the export of information and data, integrating the scientific legacy of the South into the intellectual production managed and controlled by the North.


The dependence of African academics on international journals and their reviewers has a well-documented negative impact on academic autonomy. Echoing Hountondji, Nyamnjoh rightly 

argues

 that the African academy continues to suffer from endemic reliance on external validation through Northern journals.


Jean-François Bayart criticised Hountondji and dependency theory for not properly historicising societies. Bayart developed the concept of extraversion in a new and different way, focusing on the political agency of African elites. He argued that in unequal environments elite actors, such as NGOs, may deliberately deploy ‘financial extraversion’ to mobilise donor aid. His work emphasises the actions of private foreign actors, or multinational companies, that capture Africa’s trade with Europe for purposes of commercial gain, exacerbating Africa’s dependence.  


The fall and rise of multinational publishers


During the late colonial period, British multinationals dominated publishing in anglophone Africa. Their presence expanded in the postcolonial period due to increased demand for educational materials in the newly independent states. Most multinational operators withdrew in the financial crisis of the 1980s as textbooks became increasingly unaffordable.


Where once Macmillan and Oxford University Press controlled textbook markets, including in apartheid South Africa, the company with the largest academic footprint today is Taylor & Francis (T&F). Exploiting the market opportunities brought about by the end of apartheid from the mid-1990s, T&F has taken over the publishing of over 70 Africa-related journals, setting up co-publishing agreements with the University of South Africa and launching many new journals.


More recently, T&F has been publishing a rapidly growing number of papers in its ‘mega’ journals modelled on those of the science publishers. Around 40% of articles published in T&F’s 

Cogent Social Sciences

 are from Africa. Many of these papers are published with open access waivers or discounts funded by its partnership with the donor-funded EIFL. T&F

reports

 that since 2020 more than 18,000 researchers have received either 50% discounts or complete fee waivers to publish in its journals.


The library at the Cheikh Anta Diop University in Dakar, Senegal (Wikimedia Commons, 2008)


R4L …

author: Ahmed Ashmawy, Haitham Gabr
title: ‘They’ll go a second time, a third, a fourth’: The battlefield Wadi al-Mollak’s farm laborers can’t but return to
content:
In the daily battle to put bread on the table, buy cooking gas, pay for education and healthcare, the daily battle to provide for the basic necessities of life, the farm laborers of the Wadi al-Mollak village in Sharqiya fight without land, schools, hospitals, roads or transportation fit for humans, without drinking water or a sanitation system, without work that can guarantee subsistence, let alo

ne a “Hayah Karima.”

 


And yet everyone fights. Men, youth and children are packed every day by the dozens into the dabbaba (tank), as the open-bed pickup truck is known. They set off at the first light of dawn along a deadly road they have no choice but to take. They head to the large farms within the village or in Ismailia, to earn enough to get by and keep fighting.


That is why when their sons come back from the battlefield as lifeless bodies, instead of bringing home the little they had gone out to earn, the tragedy is more than the loss of loved ones. It is an utter defeat that can take years to overcome.


So we saw it on our visit to Ezbet al-Dawoudiya, one of dozens of similar ezbas in Wadi al-Mollak. 


We arrived on Thursday. Two days earlier, a dabbaba carrying some of Dawoudiya’s residents to work at mango

farms


belonging

to the Armed Forces’ National Service Projects Organizations in the Abu Sultan area of Ismailia collided with another coming from the opposite direction from the Bahr al-Baqar village, carrying boys and girls to other farms in the same area. The collision

killed 19 people

, including one person from Dawoudiya whom the residents tell us succumbed to his injuries on Saturday. Twenty nine more people were

injured

 in the crash.


In total, 12 of the village’s young men and children were killed and six others injured, some critically.


***


“We want to go to the funeral,” we tell the driver of the dabbaba, the only way to get to the ezbas of the village.


“Which funeral?” he asks. “The one in Abu Ghazbawy, Abu Agwa or Shelh? There’s one or two dead in each. The group funeral was Wednesday. The governor came and all the big shots.”


Following the advice of the women sitting beside us in the truck, we decide to go to Dawoudiya, the ezba with the largest number of victims: eight killed and six injured, residents would tell us later.


The truck sets off along a partly paved road no more than four meters wide, running between two canals. There were no street lights. Every time we hit a bump or a pothole, we grip the truck’s metal rails tighter.


Day laborers in Wadi al-Mollak do not only work in the mango harvest during the summer. Throughout the year, they also pick fruit in the large citrus farms surrounding them, or they sort and pack produce at export stations in Beheira and Alexandria, village residents will tell us later. The workers are taken to those farms and stations in the same open pick-ups they use to reach the mango farms.


Most of the land in Wadi al-Mollak once belonged to

Arabia for Land Reclamation

, established in the 1960s. The farm laborers called it the “Yugoslav company” because it brought in experts and equipment for desert land reclamation from Yugoslavia.


“When I was young, I used to work as a day laborer for the company. I would earn a quarter of a pound,” a man in his seventies from Mollak recalls. “Then, in the 1990s, we woke up one day to find out they had

sold

large areas of the land to businessmen. We don’t know how. And we’re the people who live here, we didn’t even get a single

qirat

(175 square meters)


of the land.”


On our way to Dawoudiya, we listen to the women’s grievances, which pour out after they learn we are on a reporting assignment.


They first lament “the youth who die just to earn their daily bread,” then the rising prices and lack of services. They point to the road, which they say has remained in the same condition for years. As crashes kept happening there, residents have repeatedly requested it be finished and one of the canals be covered to widen it. But their calls went unheeded until Wednesday, when the local administrative unit added a layer of sand to the road to make it easier for the high-end cars carrying officials to reach the site of the group funeral.


The women stop talking only to point out the funeral sites along both sides of the road, each one as we pass it.


“Here, there was a funeral. Two died. And here, there was another funeral. One or two died. So-and-so’s sons.”


When we reach Dawoudiya, a …

author: Mohamed Amin Abdishukri Maalim
title: Kenya’s Market in Political Violence and the Road to the 2027 Election
content:
On the afternoon of 17 June 2025, I witnessed a large group of young men riding into central Nairobi on motorbikes carrying whips and clubs. They had come to break up a demonstration over the death of Albert Ojwang, a 31-year-old teacher and blogger who had

died in police custody

earlier that month after being arrested over allegations that he had posted defamatory content on X about the Deputy Inspector General of Police. The young men beat whoever they caught while officers of the National Police Service stood by. Kenyans call them goons, young men paid to disrupt, intimidate and injure on a politician’s behalf. Kenya has, without announcing it to itself, built a market in political violence and the logic of this market points toward the formation of militias before the general election of August 2027. 


A rate card for disorder


In November 2025, the research firm Odipo Dev and the civic collective Tribeless Youth published a

report

 of a trade that runs like any gig economy with a rate card priced by the seniority of the buyer: KSh500 to disrupt a protest for a ward representative, KSh1,500 for the same job commissioned by a member of parliament, KSh2,000 by a governor, and KSh2,500 by a businessman, while a land seizure fetches between KSh1,500 and KSh2,000. A recruiter typically manages between ten and thirty young men. The average recruit clears less than KSh10,000 a month, and the recruiters and handlers can take in hundreds of thousands of shillings during an election season. Payment is made in hard cash just before the job, usually at petrol stations, to avoid traceability. Recruiters work both on the ground, at the “base” and at

boda boda

 stages,

matatu

 (public transport buses) termini, bars and football pitches, and digitally through WhatsApp groups. The National Cohesion and Integration Commission (NCIC),

 tracing the evolution of Kenya’s gangs in 2025

, describes online gangs that exploit the anonymity, reach and speed of the internet to recruit members, coordinate operations and incite violence, and names X, Facebook, WhatsApp and TikTok as central to gang recruitment and mobilization.


The supply side of this market is demography. The World Bank

estimates

 that about 800,000 Kenyans enter the labour market every year to compete for roughly 100,000 formal jobs, and the Federation of Kenya Employers

estimates that two-thirds

 of the country’s unemployed are under the age of thirty-five. According to the

 Kenya National Bureau of Statistics

, 83 per cent of Kenyans work in the informal economy. In July 2026, AFP

interviewed young Kenyans,

 and they spoke the language of labour more than politics. “You end up being a goon to at least earn something,” said one, a 27-year-old from one of the largest informal settlements in Nairobi who has been a goon since he was seventeen. Another, a 28-year-old criminology graduate, summed the situation up in a sentence, saying, “They say education is the key, but honestly speaking we never find the padlock open.”


The demand side is politics, and this is the recorded finding of the state’s own institutions. NCIC

research

 concluded in 2017 that almost 90 per cent of Kenya’s organized criminal gangs were financed and deployed by politicians. Its 2025 report on the evolution of those gangs found most members aged between 15 and 35, with some recruits as young as 11. In April 2026, the Interior Cabinet Secretary, Kipchumba Murkomen,

told

 a Senate committee that more than 104 criminal gangs were active in the country under the patronage of politicians. By that point, the police claimed to have arrested over 300 suspects. No politician was among them. The former president of the Law Society of Kenya, Faith Odhiambo,

calls

 the result a procurement system of violence saying, “The goons and criminal gangs have been allowed to run a parallel economy with well-known buyers and sellers; until we prosecute the buyers, the market remains open.”


A lineage of hired youth


The 1960s independence-era single parties in Africa kept youth wings who the political scientist Andreas Mehler described as “often nothing but a group of thugs”. When multiparty democracy returned to Kenya in 1992, the ruling party KANU built Youth for KANU ‘92 (YK92), a group that was accused of buying votes and intimidating opponents. Among its organizers and enforcers was a young William Ruto, the current president of Kenya. The same years brought the ethnic clashes in the Rift …

author: Namonje Izukanji Namukonda
title: Africa’s Youth Employment Crisis Has a Curriculum Problem
content:
When I worked for The Harvest Fund, I sat across from women-farmers who had just completed training in milling, business development, food safety. Competent women. Women who had shown up every day, taken notes, asked questions. And then, when we asked them what they wanted to do next what they wanted to build some of them went blank. Not because they lacked intelligence. Not because they lacked ambition. But because nobody had ever told them that their ambition was allowed to be that large. Owning a hammer mill sounded, to some of them, like something that happened to other people. People who were not them.I used to find this frustrating. I no longer do. Because I understand now what was actually happening in that room. We had taught them a skill. We had not given them a job.


There is a sequence that development gets wrong so consistently that we have stopped noticing it. It goes like this: identify a population facing economic exclusion, train them in a skill or a trade, encourage them to start a business or join a cooperative, measure the number of businesses registered, declare the intervention a success. What this sequence skips entirely is the middle. The part where a person becomes a worker before they are expected to become an employer. The part where they learn not in a classroom but on an actual job what it means to show up with accountability, to make a mistake and correct it, to develop pride in a process, to understand the difference between being paid and being exploited.


Across sub-Saharan Africa, our empowerment architecture has been built almost entirely on the first and third stages of this sequence. Training. Then entrepreneurship. The middle employment  is treated as optional. As though it is a luxury that communities in poverty cannot afford to wait for. I want to argue the opposite. The middle is not a luxury. It is the foundation. And without it, both the training and the entrepreneurship tend to collapse. Africa is projected to have the world’s largest workforce by 2050. One-quarter of the global labour force will be African. The continent’s response in development programming, in government policy, in the billions spent annually on livelihood interventions has largely been to prepare that workforce for self-employment.


We train farmers to own agribusinesses. We train women to run cooperatives. We train youth to be entrepreneurs. And then we count the outputs: loans disbursed, businesses registered, products sold. What we almost never measure is whether any of these people have ever held a structured job. Whether they have ever been employees. Whether they have ever had the experience of being paid regularly, managed accountably, and given the space to develop mastery in a role before being handed the responsibility of running an enterprise.


The result is that our outcome numbers look reasonable on paper and feel hollow on the ground. I have seen it. I have measured it. Three or four women from a cohort of sixty thriving independently and we celebrate the three or four without asking what happened to the fifty-six. What happened to the fifty-six is that we handed them the third floor of a building and forgot to build the first two.


In May 2026, Msitu360 launched Feeding Msitu a school feeding programme at Chainda Community School in Lusaka serving 132 children daily. The programme is staffed by four women we call the Mamas. The Mamas are not volunteers. They are not community mothers giving time they do not have in exchange for goodwill and a certificate of participation. They are paid, contracted, trained workers with regular salaries, defined working hours, and weekends off. They receive food safety training. They work within a nutritionally designed menu developed by a qualified nutritionist. They are employees. This is, in the context of African school feeding programmes, unusual. The dominant model across the continent relies on unpaid community labour typically women to prepare and serve meals. It is called community participation. It is, more accurately, the extraction of women’s labour under a different name.


At Msitu360, we made a different choice. Not because we have more money than other programmes, but because we hold a different thesis: that the meal is the proof of the employment model, not the other way around. The product we are building is not nutrition. The product is dignified, paid, certified employment for African women. The meals are what that employment …

author: Noziphiwo Sigwela
title: Public land for the public good: Tafelberg ruling puts Cape Town on notice
content:
On the 2

nd

 of July 2026, the Constitutional Court handed down an unanimous judgement that will reshape how we understand the right to housing in South Africa.


The Tafelberg judgment (

Adonisi v Minister for Transport and Public Works, Western Cape; Minister of Human Settlements v Minister for Transport and Public Works, Western Cape

 [2026] ZACC 29 (2 July 2026)

) declared the 2015 sale of the Tafelberg property at 353 Main Road, Sea Point, Cape Town, unlawful.


This ruling highlighted the failure by the Western Cape government and City of Cape Town to fulfil their constitutional duties to redress spatial injustice by providing affordable housing in well-located areas. This battle was championed by urban land movement,

Reclaim the City

, with support from NGO,

Ndifuna Ukwazi

. In a celebrated outcome, both levels of government were ordered to submit detailed reports to the high court within three months (2 October 2026).


But as we celebrate this victory, we must confront the sobering truth. This was only one of the City’s many failures. The same week the Constitutional Court affirmed the importance of spatial justice, the Public Protector released a devastating report on the City’s failure to provide basic municipal services to Langa Flats in Langa and in the township of Khayelitsha. The contrast could not be clearer. While the city and provincial governments fought for a decade to sell off prime public land in Sea Point, residents in Langa and Khayelitsha have been living without functioning sewers, fire safety equipment, clean water, and without the dignity that the constitution promises them.


Two cities, one constitution


The Public Protector’s report,

Systemic Investigation into Alleged Failure by the City of Cape Town to Provide Basic Municipal Services in Langa Flats and Khayelitsha Township

, reads like an indictment of a city that has forgotten half its residents.


In Langa Flats, sewer infrastructure has been in a state of disrepair for 14 years. Firehose reels and extinguishers that were promised to be repaired in March 2022 are still broken.


Residents have been forced to contribute R100 per household to hire cleaners for communal areas, a responsibility that rightfully belongs to the municipality. Housing units have cracked walls that, despite repeated commitments, are years later still to be assessed.


According to the report by the Public Protector, Town Two Clinic does not have smoke detectors or CCTV cameras. Earlier this year, the security company at the clinic fell victim to extortion rackets that are ravaging the community.


In Khayelitsha, the picture is no better. At SST-Marikana, residents who were relocated by the City to make way for sewer repairs were moved to a site without access to electricity or adequate water.


In multiple inspections of the area, the Public Protector found none of the 143 water taps that the City claimed to have provided. Relocated families relied on a self-connected communal tap – a pipe pressed down with a cement block, providing only a trickle of water.


An elderly wheelchair-bound resident was left alone without accessible water or electricity, in conditions “neither safe nor conducive to his health and wellbeing”.


At the

Matthew Goniwe

 and

Town Two

 clinics, there were no smoke detectors, and no functional CCTV cameras, with paper records stored in rooms without fire detection. Staff at

Matthew Goniwe

 reported that the clinic could go without electricity for two to three weeks at a time. This is not a failure of resources alone, but a failure of

priorities

.


The spatial logic of neglect


What connects Tafelberg to Langa and Khayelitsha is not just geography but a spatial logic that has persisted since Apartheid. Well-located land in Sea Point is fiercely protected for the wealthy, while poor and working-class communities are pushed to the urban periphery and are neglected there – out of sight, out of mind!


The Constitutional Court’s Tafelberg judgment recognised this explicitly. Justice Mhlantla, in her judgment, said that the location of housing must be treated as a “relevant factor” in decisions about public land, particularly where such decisions affect efforts to redress apartheid spatial injustice.


But spatial justice is not only about where housing is built, it is also about how communities are

served

 once they are there. The Public Protector’s report reveals a pattern of systematic neglect that mirrors the …

author: Nabil Ferdaoussi
title: A border spectacle
content:
What happened last Thursday in Ceuta was a

border spectacle

 of surprising scale and scope. Tens of thousands of mainly young fellow Moroccans stormed the gates while others braved the water to enter the enclave. All the elements of the spectacle were there: from images of boisterous youngsters jockeying for entry, to a diplomatic slanging match, to border patrols scrambling to push migrants back to Morocco.

It sounds like a geopolitical déjà vu — almost the same border antics: scene, actors, protagonists, and victims staged in May 2021. In fact, what happened in Ceuta is the third episode of the border spectacle: the first staged in May 2021, the second in September 2024, and here we are watching the third — and perhaps not the last — episode, marking a shift in Morocco’s migration diplomacy to a more coercive approach.

There is no conspiracy theory behind the Ceuta border spectacle; there is only a geopolitical buildup to understand Morocco’s coercive migration diplomacy. The latter has shifted migration governance from policies, practices, and discourses to the direct use of its youth and other racialized African migrants in diplomatic sparring.

Here is the buildup: On December 10, 2020, the Trump administration recognized Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara. This historic moment led Morocco to garner further diplomatic recognition, especially from its traditional allies — not least Spain as a former colonizer. In January 2021, a diplomatic logjam between Morocco and Germany started to simmer following the latter’s criticism of Donald Trump’s proclamation to recognize Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. This diplomatic friction with Germany prompted Morocco to push the European Union.

Meanwhile, the possibility of meeting Morocco’s expectations, whether by the EU or its member states, proved far-fetched. The diplomatic spat between Morocco and Spain reached its nadir when the latter hosted Brahim Ghali, the leader of the Polisario Front, in April 2021 to seek medical treatment. In a tit-for-tat response, Morocco unleashed over 8,000 migrants, including around 3,000 minors. Santiago Abascal, the leader of the anti-migrant far-right Vox party in Spain, denounced the arrivals, stating Morocco was “launching minors like battering rams” against the Spanish borders.

Now, the same scenario is unfolding after Pedro Sánchez visited Algeria to parley with President Abdelmajid Tebboune over natural gas and Western Sahara.

In Europe, the border spectacle sparked a moral panic that feared the invasion of the southern flanks of Europe, raking up right-wing opprobrium over Sánchez’s progressive yet lax migration policies. Far from being an invasion, the border spectacle staged produced anti-migration fodder for far-right politicians.

The border spectacle has resurfaced the centuries-old colonization of Ceuta and Melilla.

The international public that redeems Sánchez as the proponent of the Palestinian cause and progressive migration reforms is bewildered by Ceuta’s tiny geography at the outer fringe of the African continent, wondering how Spain, and for that matter Europe, will be invaded while in Africa. Some historical context is urgent here to disentangle these “only land borders between Africa and EUrope.”

Depending on one’s geopolitical stance, Ceuta and Melilla are at once enclaves and exclaves. From the colonial standpoint of Spain and the European Union, they are seen as exclaves, embodying the external sovereign extension of Spain and, more recently, Europe. In most academic literature, however, the two cities are enclaves standing as the last remnants of European colonization on the African continent. For Moroccans, the two cities are occupied territories, whose recovery remains an unfinished national project of decolonization.

The dispute over Ceuta and Melilla has shaped a long history of sporadic tensions in the relationship between Morocco and Spain. Its historical roots extend back to the Reconquista (c. 718–1492), culminating in the fall of Al-Andalus, and ended with the expulsion of the Moors, between 718 and 1492, from the Iberian Peninsula to North Africa.

Spain extended its sovereignty beyond the Peninsula to vie for external territorial sovereignty in North Africa, seizing Melilla in 1497 and Ceuta — initially conquered by Portugal in 1415 and then ceded to Spain — in 1668. The two towns served as external bulwarks for the clash between the

Ummah

 of Islam and Christendom. Well …

author: Mark Blackburn
title: Tribunal rejects federal government’s request to add panelists to First Nations child welfare case
content:
The chair of the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal (Tribunal) has turned down

a request from the federal government

 to add two new commissioners to a panel hearing a case of reforming the First Nations child welfare system across the country.


“The Chairperson has reviewed the parties’ submissions in response to the AGC’s panel recomposition,” wrote a short reply from chair Jennifer Khurana and released by the registrar. “The AGC’s [Attorney General of Canada] request is dismissed.


According to the chair, reasons she dismissed the request will follow.


In July, the federal government requested that Khurara add two new commissioners to the panel overseeing a discrimination case against the federal government over child welfare on reserves and Jordan’s Principle.


When the Tribunal started hearing the case in 2012, the panel consisted of members Sophie Marchildon, Réjean Bélanger and Edward Lustig. Bélanger died suddenly in 2015, leaving just two to oversee the case. 

Lustig resigned on July 7,

 leaving just Marchildon.


According to the government, the case has gotten more complex since Bélanger’s death and requested that the chair not allow Marchildon to continue on her own.


First Nations organizations including the First Nations Child and Family Caring Society (Caring Society) and the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) the two groups that started the complaint back in 2007, argued adding two new commissioners now would cause delays in the process.


In 2016, the Tribunal ruled that Canada discriminated against First Nations children by knowingly underfunding programs that were supposed to help them. They ordered the discrimination to end immediately and that all sides work together to come up with a plan to reform the system.


A decade later, Marchildon is now reviewing a plan put forward by the federal government and another by a group called the National Children’s Chiefs’ Commission – a body commissioned by chiefs across the country.


Cindy Blackstock, executive director of the Caring Society, told APTN News in August that it joined the Commission “in expressing our deep concern regarding Canada’s attempts to disrupt the Tribunal’s decision-making process at this late stage as it will undoubtedly cause delays (and harms) for children.”


“This unnecessary maneuver comes at a time when we have proceedings underway to enforce Canada’s legal obligation to not discriminate against children relating to Jordan’s Principle and child and family.”


The AFN argued that “an entire generation has passed; children born when this Complaint was first brought in 2007 are now adults with children of their own. Yet Canada has still not implemented the necessary remedy to address systemic discrimination against First Nations children and youth.


“Any step that risks delaying a final, effective and durable remedy must be avoided.”


Canada is also requesting that Marchildon not be allowed to issue a written document of reasons why the panel approved the Ontario Final Agreement – an $8.4 billion agreement between First Nations in Ontario and the federal government to turn responsibility of the child welfare system to communities.


Khurara said that decision will come later.


The post

Tribunal rejects federal government’s request to add panelists to First Nations child welfare case

 appeared first on

APTN News

.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: US Sanctioning ICC Prosecutor Who Reportedly Worked on Warrant for Netanyahu
content:
The Trump administration has sanctioned numerous ICC figures who have worked on cases against Israeli officials.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced on Tuesday that the U.S. is imposing sanctions on two key figures in the International Criminal Court (ICC), including a prosecutor who has led charges against top Israeli government officials like Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The U.S. is sanctioning ICC President Tomoko Akane, from Japan, and ICC prosecutor Abdoulaye Seye, of Senegal, Rubio announced, as part of the U.S.’s assault on the international tribunal.

Rubio did not give specific reasons as to why those individuals have been chosen, but said that they have “directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction.”

In his statement, Rubio claims the sanctions are about protecting U.S. sovereignty. Indeed, the U.S. has long stood in opposition to the ICC as the court has sought, amid its flaws, to hold to account war criminals and genocidaires across the world.

However, the sanctions also appear targeted at punishing those who have prosecuted Israeli officials. Seye, a senior trial attorney, was on the team of prosecutors who sought an arrest warrant for Netanyahu for crimes against humanity in Gaza.

Israeli media also claims that Seye has led prosecution efforts against other Israeli officials, including an arrest warrant application filed against Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich earlier this year, Middle East Eye reported. The claims of Seye’s involvement in Smotrich’s or any other case have not been substantiated by U.S. outlets.

President Donald Trump has previously openly said that the U.S. is going after the ICC in part to “defend” Israel.

Rubio “is not trying to defend me. ​He’s trying to defend Bibi and various other people,” Trump said in July, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname. “There are many people ​that shouldn’t be looked at that way. But there is no indication that I’m one of them at this moment.”

The U.S. has also imposed sanctions — which are ruinous due to the U.S.’s power over the global banking system — on at least 11 ICC officials. These sanctions have been placed on ICC officials who have been involved in prosecution of Israeli officials as well as those who have investigated members of the U.S. forces for crimes in Afghanistan.

The sanctions have been issued under Trump’s executive order issued in February 2025. However, this executive order as well as sanctions against a slate of figures like UN special rapporteur for Palestine Francesca Albanese are facing lawsuits by human rights groups.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, as political censorship from the right intensifies, we have no choice but to ask for your help.

We are fundraising right now to cover our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: GN raises Baffin Island caribou quota to 6,000
content:
The number of caribou that hunters will be allowed to harvest this season on Baffin Island has jumped dramatically following

substantial growth

 in the animal’s estimated population.


The prior hunting restriction of 550 caribou per season has now been raised to 6,000, the Nunavut Government announced Aug. 13 in a news release.


That amounts to approximately 12 per cent of the estimated population there.


This decision goes against a recommendation from researchers inside of Nunavut’s Department of Environment, who proposed a five per cent harvest rate instead, according to a report on caribou abundance estimates published in December 2025. 


There was a

moratorium

 in 2015 on barrenland caribou hunting in Baffin Island, after surveys the year prior found the population had fallen to around 4,600. Previous estimates dating from the 1980s had placed numbers at an estimated 150,000.


Current estimates place the the Baffin Island barrenland caribou population at nearly 49,000.


Under the new rules, wildlife authorities are also no longer placing any limits on the number of female caribou that can be harvested in the region. Previously, female caribou could only take up 20 per cent of all harvests, and hunting females with calves was banned. 


In 2025, Department of Environment researchers had recommended against that, arguing hunting limits placed on female caribou and calves should be maintained. Their research was based on recent aerial surveys.


The current caribou hunting season on Baffin Island began on July 1 and will last until June 30, 2027.


The Nunavut Wildlife Management Board agreed to increase the harvest to 6,000 caribou on June 25 after the government submitted a request that recommended the change.


The Environment Department could not be reached for comment on this story.


The board spoke with Government of Nunavut researchers, the Qikiqtaaluk Wildlife Board, Nunavut Tunngavik Incorporated, and hunters and trappers organizations in Igloolik, Kinngait and Pangnirtung, according to board documents.


Some members had, however, expressed concerns allowing 12 per cent of the population to be hunted could pose “an unusual and largely unprecedented level of risk” to the caribou in Baffin Island.


“Board members noted that this harvest rate is high compared with other Nunavut caribou herds,” board chairperson Daniel Shewchuk wrote to Brian Koonoo, Nunavut’s environment minister. 


The Nunavut Wildlife Management Board did not respond to requests for comment for this story. 


Under the new rules, caribou hunters are also no longer being asked to submit samples of their game to their local wildlife office or hunting and trapping organization. They are just asked to report how many they harvested. 


Each hunting and trapping organization is responsible for allocating the share of the caribou hunting tags within their communities.

author: Valerie Anne
title: Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat Joke About Rebooting ‘Twilight’ but Bella Is Gay This Time
content:
During their press tour for their upcoming stoner buddy comedy The Wrong Girls, Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat stopped by Bravo studios for Watch What Happens Live. During the interview, Andy Cohen asks a question from a fan about Kristen saying she would reboot Twilight, and Kristen says she was mostly joking but would consider doing a continuation vs. a re-hashing of the source material. Alia Shawkat jumps in and jokes, “Bella would come back and be like ‘I’m gay,” which makes Kristen Stewart double over with laughter. Alia goes on to joke it would be “hot, modern, fresh” and they encourage Kristen’s wife Dylan Meyer to write it, and she jokes that she already has while standing in the bartender spot on the set.

Kristen Stewart goes on to joke that Bella would say, “I’m gonna fuck your whole family” and then realizes she’s never actually said that phrase before but, “God, it feels good.”

And this, friends, is why queer people should be in charge of everything.

It’s no surprise they wanted to recruit Dylan Meyer for this imaginary project, because she wrote The Wrong Girls; it’s her directorial debut, and Kristen Stewart has said she loved working with her wife. The feeling was mutual, with Dylan having only good things to say about working with Kristen. Alia Shawkat even joined in the lovefest, saying Dylan “was such a great leader, so calm and grounded and appreciative of everybody’s time and clear about what she wanted”

All in all, this trio seems like they’re on fire, so why NOT get them to reboot the Twilight series, but gayer this time. They can play vampire kickball instead of baseball this time, and it will be wonderful.
